design.routeDecision: Build separate outer returns before waking the middle roamer, or connect the islands and share an escape corridor?

design.captureConsequence: The relay adds a non-scoring permanent return; erosion may restore arrows only on the earned side routes.
design.counterplay: Use the protected connector as a fallback and follow erosion and lane warnings. Neither forces a repair before another route is available.
design.lesson: Combine known arrow, erosion and relay rules: foundations and opened connectors are permanent; earned marked territory can reactivate.
design.mastery: Use the protected connector and reclaim both side currents before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The center connector stays dependable while a reopened current visibly changes a side route.
design.routeDecision: Secure the permanent return first or invest in an earned sideways shortcut that erosion may reopen into an arrow field?

design.captureConsequence: A line-only first cut establishes a permanent return lane for later enclosures.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: Two occupied regions can keep their field even though the closing line is reclaimed.
design.mastery: Create and then use a line-only return lane.
design.memorableMoment: The board explains why both occupied sides remain dark.
design.routeDecision: Separate the two keepers first or wait until they share one side?

design.captureConsequence: The marked shortcut becomes ordinary-speed reclaimed ground. The roamer may now use it too, so the outer stepping platforms retain their value.
design.counterplay: The first broad arrow has a clear landing and no forced turn. Leave the locked column before it fires; retain a second departure when reclaiming the roamer.
design.lesson: A direct arrow route can be efficient without being the best return after a capture. The locked lane and awakened ground domain remain separately readable.
design.mastery: Connect and visit the upper and lower stepping platforms before clearing without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The fastest outward route turns into contested reclaimed ground, making the quieter stepping return useful.
design.routeDecision: Use the fast long crossing toward the middle landing, or claim the upper stepping platform before awakening the ground roamer?

design.captureConsequence: A newly connected work mat extends both your return network and the roamer movement domain.
design.counterplay: Keep a parallel aisle and choose the next departure before the sleeper becomes active.
design.lesson: Opening the board can activate a new threat on reclaimed ground; the warning gives time to leave.
design.mastery: Use three different work mats after waking the roamer.
design.memorableMoment: The best new shortcut becomes a shared route with a visibly awakening threat.
design.routeDecision: Reclaim the middle aisle now and wake its roamer, or join an outer work mat first to preserve another escape?

design.captureConsequence: A small return establishes an approach around a shelf without necessarily reclaiming its far pocket. Keep earning ground if a pickup expires; another eligible anchor may offer a later window.
design.counterplay: Outer keepers move along readable vertical lanes; inner keepers cross diagonally around the shelves. Time the outer crossing and use either end of the tall islands for a return. Walls never close cuts.
design.lesson: A pickup collected in one chamber can help the other pilot, but neither chamber alone supplies the quota.
design.mastery: Collect the shared slow while your partner is cutting, then clear with a return closure from each pilot and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: One craft reaches a contested outer slow window while the other commits to an enclosure beside the opposite shelf.
design.routeDecision: Bank an inner approach beside the shelf, work the contested outer pocket, or shape the other chamber while your partner takes the bonus detour?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing removes live impacts and neutralizes terrain, but may activate a new ground threat without disabling either emitter.
design.counterplay: Shorten the live trail before the marked cross fires and leave an exit on reclaimed ground before capturing the roamer.
design.lesson: Combine known lane, impact and reclaimed-ground threats. Moving enemies and an active lane both send visible fronts; direct craft contact remains immediate.
design.mastery: Clear without a life loss after closing an active-impact cut while the roamer was already active.
design.memorableMoment: A timely closure extinguishes a moving impact while the new ground still offers an escape from the roamer.
design.routeDecision: Spend the rest window linking another refuge, or close a smaller cut and preserve a corridor before the roamer wakes?

design.captureConsequence: Each occupied chamber retains independently; a capture cannot collect the shared pickup. Keep making useful cuts when a window is missed.
design.counterplay: Watch both keepers before choosing a side to bank. The divider has opposite-facing shelves: go around their tips and use either end of the tall islands for a return. Walls are never landings.
design.lesson: A pickup collected in one chamber can help the other pilot, but neither chamber alone supplies the quota.
design.mastery: Collect the shared slow while your partner is cutting, then clear with a return closure from each pilot and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: One pilot touches the slow symbol while the partner completes a long enclosure on the far side of the divider.
design.routeDecision: Spend a short detour on the shared slow window while your partner cuts the opposite chamber, or bank both islands first?

design.captureConsequence: Reclaimed corners become alternative launch ground instead of decorative completion cleanup.
design.counterplay: Stay on a landing while reading a lock, then cross toward a reachable return. Enclose lethal corners before flying through them.
design.lesson: Keep the two open junctions useful. Corner terrain changes approach cost while the locked column can cut across both.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal corners and connect all three foundations without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: A short connector changes which side of the junction can be crossed in one rest window.
design.routeDecision: Bridge a short gap into an outer rail, or first reclaim one corner to give the next crossing a different approach?

design.captureConsequence: Progress in one occupied district does not silently fill the other; both remain readable capture problems.
design.counterplay: Choose a departure behind the frontier patrol, then change districts instead of defending an unimportant lost cell.
design.lesson: Each district retains its own eroder. The permanent center lane separates their field domains and never erodes.
design.mastery: Close a cut in each district and neutralize the eastern hazard without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The reliable center lane lets you switch priorities when pressure builds on one side.
design.routeDecision: Develop the slow western district first, or make a larger eastern enclosure around the marked hazard?

design.captureConsequence: An enclosure neutralizes the bank immediately, but route resilience depends on which foundations you connect.
design.counterplay: Keep the next permanent return in view, repair a valuable gap, and do not treat cooled terrain as permanently protected.
design.lesson: Lanes and erosion use separate warnings. Foundations never erode; reclaimed hazards can reactivate if earned territory reopens.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal banks, connect all four foundations and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A permanent alternate return remains available when an earned frontier is marked for erosion.
design.routeDecision: Use an earned shortcut across a cooled bank or connect permanent landings before erosion can reopen that route?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. Field-retaining enemies still determine which regions remain unclaimed, and the existing terrain or patrol consequences remain active.
design.counterplay: Lock the interceptor onto an expendable approach, turn toward a broad connection, and leave an escape corridor for the roamer that activates after capture.
design.lesson: Interception pressures the current heading while capture can wake a different movement-domain threat; solve the two roles with different routes.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal banks and close a cut after the roamer activates without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One turn defeats the committed intercept, neutralizes a hazardous bank, and wakes pressure on the newly reclaimed route.
design.routeDecision: Feint toward the northern clear channel, or turn south after the lock while preserving room for the reclaimed-ground roamer?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting two bays can make one useful return network while the remaining bay stays a separate route choice.
design.counterplay: Every mouth is broad; use outside routes instead of following a patrol through a narrow return.
design.lesson: An open mouth is unclaimed field, not a safe doorway. Closing it changes both retention and contour connections.
design.mastery: Connect all three bay foundations without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Three interrupted contours can be joined in different orders without clearing five repetitive boxes.
design.routeDecision: Bridge the nearby bays for several returns, or approach the distant bay before its frontier patrol arrives?

design.captureConsequence: A connection shortens your return but can also enlarge a roamer’s movement domain.
design.counterplay: Use the three unequal landings and choose when to connect them; no bonus or timer forces the order.
design.lesson: Only reclaimed ground supports an active roamer. An unclaimed gap can keep two return networks separate.
design.mastery: Connect all three landings after activating at least one roamer, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Joining useful landings has a visible cost as a formerly isolated threat gains more room.
design.routeDecision: Join the nearby berths before waking their sleepers, or isolate one side and keep the far return clear?

design.captureConsequence: The first reclaimed bed determines which side offers a shorter, faster next route.
design.counterplay: Return to either end of the spine; the optional life is not needed to complete the board.
design.lesson: Reclaimed routes stay fast even when the adjacent unclaimed approach is slow.
design.mastery: Reclaim one entire slow bed before crossing the other.
design.memorableMoment: Two apparently symmetric sides offer different return distances from the interior start.
design.routeDecision: Use the central spine to enclose one slow bed first, or take a larger route around both?

design.captureConsequence: A connection can send frontier pressure around one frame while the other remains open.
design.counterplay: Leave the bridge away from the frontier patrol and preserve the opposite side as a return option.
design.lesson: Open frames are not separate capture rules: only keeper positions decide retained regions.
design.mastery: Make a closure from each lens landing.
design.memorableMoment: One shared bridge supports two different chamber problems.
design.routeDecision: Work inward toward one lens landing, or close around the outside of both open frames?

design.captureConsequence: A secured connection shelters the craft from the lane, while the stationary emitter continues retaining its field region.
design.counterplay: Watch the marked row and close on the landing before the attack. Start the next crossing after the active lane clears.
design.lesson: A lane locks to your row, warns, then fires. Moving the craft out is not enough if the unfinished trail still crosses it.
design.mastery: Clear without a life loss after closing a cut whose exposed trail crossed a warning lane.
design.memorableMoment: The first cut closes after the lock appears and before the lane fires.
design.routeDecision: Close on the landing during the warning, or carry a longer exposed trail toward the far border?

design.captureConsequence: Each added connection shortens both partners’ routes, but an enclosure can also introduce pressure on that connection.
design.counterplay: The middle wall has two distinct bypasses. Keep the lethal pocket outside cuts until enclosed and avoid funneling both craft into the same active roamer. Coordinate the Interceptor around exposed lines and the Disruptor around moving threats; neither pulse substitutes for the other.
design.lesson: Combine known return networks, material decisions and wake-up timing without learning another rule.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers and connect both intermediate islands to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Four separated islands become a shared network with two moving reclaimed-ground threats.
design.routeDecision: Reach opposite stepping islands first, or connect along one flank and let a partner reopen the other approach?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. The adapted actor still retains its occupied field region, while the existing wall, foundation and patrol rules remain unchanged.
design.counterplay: Keep both lens landings available, draw the lock away from the chosen return, and use closure to cancel interception before reshaping the frontier.
design.lesson: The frontier patrol follows the changing boundary while the interceptor follows only a previously locked heading target.
design.mastery: Cancel interception and make a return from both lens landings.
design.memorableMoment: One capture defeats a committed intercept and redirects a separate frontier threat around the other lens.
design.routeDecision: Shape the bridge frontier before provoking interception, or feint into one open lens and turn toward the opposite landing after lock?

design.captureConsequence: A successful bridge can neutralize terrain, join foundations and redirect a patrol in the same capture.
design.counterplay: Use broad outside bypasses, choose one patrol at a time, and capture marked field before treating it as return ground.
design.lesson: Known slow, lethal, field-retention and frontier rules combine; the rings do not introduce a new surface.
design.mastery: Connect all three rings and neutralize both marked bridges without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Three broken circuits become one readable reclaimed network through a chosen sequence of cuts.
design.routeDecision: Connect the three rings along the long clear outside, or neutralize the marked bridges to form a shorter return circuit?

design.captureConsequence: Material neutralization and roamer activation can occur in the same enclosure; both partners must read the changed board.
design.counterplay: Use the side spines to change departure heights. Enclose crosses before entering them and leave space around the courtyard when a roamer wakes. Coordinate the Interceptor around exposed lines and the Disruptor around moving threats; neither pulse substitutes for the other.
design.lesson: Removing a terrain hazard does not make every reclaimed route free of enemies.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers and connect the courtyard to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: A dangerous garden becomes passable just as the tracked bodies make the surrounding ground busy.
design.routeDecision: Neutralize the upper hazard before linking the courtyard, or establish the lower slow-field approach while the partner prepares a different exit?

design.captureConsequence: A bridge may secure only its line while keepers occupy both sides. The new link still gives both craft a shorter return, even when neither specialist uses Support.
design.counterplay: Watch the two keepers and close onto reclaimed ground. The Interceptor may remove a nearby travelling impact and the Disruptor may slow a nearby keeper, but first learn the shared return itself.
design.lesson: Both craft build a shared route network from separate foundations. Specialist Support is available as an optional safety tool; no pulse is required to clear this mission.
design.mastery: Both craft contribute a closure before the shared clear, without a knockdown.
design.memorableMoment: Two isolated starting islands become a shared launch corridor.
design.routeDecision: Connect the islands together, or establish opposite return routes first?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing one row opens route choices without requiring the second row to be crossed.
design.counterplay: Use the broad upper and lower bypasses, then return to a foundation or earned ground.
design.lesson: Clear lanes between lethal rows are still unclaimed field, not guaranteed return ground.
design.mastery: Neutralize at least one marked row and connect both refuges without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A long protected spine offers several departures into the same changing hazard problem.
design.routeDecision: Neutralize the nearer row from the spine, or loop around the ends to reach the far refuge first?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting foundations shortens later escape paths but also changes the patrol route.
design.counterplay: Keep both ends of a short crossing visible. Redirect the frontier away from the chosen return before extending the cut.
design.lesson: Choose a fallback destination before departing; a frontier patrol still threatens the unfinished trail immediately.
design.mastery: Connect both foundations and close a cut with an active impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The alternative landing remains reachable when the first approach becomes pressured.
design.routeDecision: Link the upper landing first or leave two separate return destinations while shaping the frontier?

design.captureConsequence: The growing network changes field and reclaimed-ground threat domains in different ways.
design.counterplay: The permanent hub cannot erode but can still host a roamer; preserve a fresh departure and do not confuse permanence with immunity from enemies.
design.lesson: Combine known erosion, anchor, roamer and frontier rules. No new mandatory mechanic.
design.mastery: Capture both anchors, make a repair and close a cut after the hub roamer activates, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A damaged network still offers a deliberate escape because its essential connections were banked.
design.routeDecision: Bank two useful connections while routing around reclaimed-ground pressure, or take a larger capture while leaving a reserve return?

design.captureConsequence: Filling beside one arm removes old edges and changes the patrol route around the other.
design.counterplay: Watch the marked patrol, return to the broad elbow, and keep the outside approach available.
design.lesson: A frontier patrol follows the changed field edge; its speed does not increase when the route gets shorter.
design.mastery: Connect both ends of the elbow to the outer perimeter without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same L-shaped return becomes a different departure after its inside corner is captured.
design.routeDecision: Close a short cut at the elbow, or use the long arm to redirect the frontier before the next departure?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing the inner aisle creates a useful return beside, not on, the obstructing trace.
design.counterplay: The broad work pads provide independent returns; do not chase the outside patrol through a narrow approach.
design.lesson: Component-like walls redirect routes without changing craft speed or controls.
design.mastery: Close from each of the two interior work pads.
design.memorableMoment: A frustrating detour becomes the shorter route once adjacent field is reclaimed.
design.routeDecision: Thread the offset circuit corridor, or accept a longer exposed cut around a trace end?

design.captureConsequence: The relay adds a non-scoring permanent return; erosion may restore arrows only on the earned side routes.
design.counterplay: Use the protected connector as a fallback and follow both warnings. Repair a side current only when it serves the planned next closure; continue through the connector instead of chasing an isolated reopened cell.
design.lesson: Combine known arrow, erosion and relay rules: foundations and opened connectors are permanent; earned marked territory can reactivate.
design.mastery: Use the protected connector and reclaim both side currents before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The center connector stays dependable while a reopened current visibly changes a side route.
design.routeDecision: Secure the permanent return first or invest in an earned sideways shortcut that erosion may reopen into an arrow field?

design.captureConsequence: A connection shortens your return but can also enlarge a roamer’s movement domain.
design.counterplay: The near sleeper wakes behind your first return. Leave its narrow connection for the broad berth; choose when to connect the far sleeper’s separate network.
design.lesson: Only reclaimed ground supports an active roamer. An unclaimed gap can keep two return networks separate.
design.mastery: Connect all three landings after activating at least one roamer, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Joining useful landings has a visible cost as a formerly isolated threat gains more room.
design.routeDecision: Connect the near sleeper’s corridor now, or establish a side return before joining the far berths?

design.captureConsequence: A neutralized band changes route efficiency without changing actor movement speeds.
design.counterplay: The central foundation is a permanent return. Keep the exposed part short; capture neutralizes terrain but merely crossing it does not.
design.lesson: Use known terrain rules while planning an impact escape. There is no new mandatory rule in this arc.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal crossbars and close a cut with an active impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A hazardous crossbar becomes the return surface for the next enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Capture a dangerous crossbar from its clear side, or take a shorter slow-band crossing to open another approach?

design.captureConsequence: The same step is a useful short closure before activation and a place to keep moving afterward.
design.counterplay: Leave both ends of the stepped platform usable and depart again when the roamer approaches.
design.lesson: A return closes the trail but does not protect the craft from an active roamer approaching along reclaimed ground.
design.mastery: Use both ends of the stepped foundation for closures after activating the roamer.
design.memorableMoment: A familiar return surface becomes a timing choice without changing the capture rule.
design.routeDecision: Return to the short upper step or the long lower arm while the warned roamer patrols the stepped foundation?

design.captureConsequence: A neutralized bed gives both pilots a full-speed approach. The three keepers preserve contested pockets around the centre.
design.counterplay: Go around the staggered wall tips. Enclose the sump from outside; use the central island as a return rather than overextending through both slow beds.
design.lesson: Shared freeze opens an enemy timing window, not permission to enter lethal field or cross your own unfinished line.
design.mastery: Collect freeze with the partner cutting, neutralize all three beds, and clear with returns from both pilots and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: A peripheral pickup holds the keepers still while a partner banks onto the centre platform.
design.routeDecision: Take a peripheral freeze window while the partner approaches the centre, or neutralize a slow bed before either makes the crossing?

design.captureConsequence: The first capture chooses which outer route becomes ordinary ground and reshapes patrol pressure.
design.counterplay: Depart through the clear center, preserving multiple returns while watching both patrol domains.
design.lesson: Slow and lethal marks have different consequences; both are neutralized by capture.
design.mastery: Neutralize both beds without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A reclaimed central cross makes the same board approachable from four directions.
design.routeDecision: Open the slower west approach first or enclose the lethal east bed while keeping the central return?

design.captureConsequence: Each connected landing shortens later exposed crossings but also gives the frontier a new route.
design.counterplay: Keep a landing at each end of the planned crossing. Read the locked column rather than chasing a countdown.
design.lesson: A column attack uses the same locked-warning rule as a row. Frontier patrols still threaten reclaimed edges and unfinished cuts.
design.mastery: Connect all three foundations and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A column attack passes through a completed connector while the next route remains available.
design.routeDecision: Establish a short westward return before extending north, or use the next rest window for the longer connection?

design.captureConsequence: Each connection removes a local speed effect and gives a new departure instead of opening an automatic chain of captures.
design.counterplay: Use the central platform to change direction without exposure; the unmarked lower approaches remain usable in either direction.
design.lesson: An interrupted line of landing platforms is not one continuous return. Check the next reclaimed segment before leaving.
design.mastery: Visit both side platforms after connecting them and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A long sideways crossing becomes a plain return lane between two platforms.
design.routeDecision: Connect a distant side platform with the arrows or make the shorter northward return before crossing the open lower field?

design.captureConsequence: An inner landing shortens a later cut without banking against a wall. Outer returns introduce reclaimed-ground pressure, and two retainers keep each chamber contested until deliberately enclosed.
design.counterplay: The top and bottom baffle ends stay open. Watch both local keepers before crossing; after waking a roamer, turn onto a different return rather than waiting on its new rail. Either partner may travel around the divider to help.
design.lesson: Each chamber offers a short changing return and a longer inner connection; opening one chamber never clears the other occupied field.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers, with each craft closing in its starting chamber and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: A quick outside escape and a protected inner receiver become two different ways to reopen the same depot.
design.routeDecision: Wake the outer return patrols for quick perimeter access, or wrap the inner baffles to establish receiver landings first?

design.captureConsequence: The western shield joins two reserved connector segments into a useful upper route while the roamer warns and then moves on reclaimed ground.
design.counterplay: Keep the lower corridor available before enclosing the roamer. The linked corner is protected from erosion and adds no earned coverage; it is a route improvement, not free score.
design.lesson: One capture can disable a shield and open a permanent connector, but an awakened ground roamer changes which return remains comfortable.
design.mastery: Traverse the opened corner before capturing the final shield, then clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A missing corner becomes a complete return route before the last shield opens.
design.routeDecision: Secure the western shield to connect the upper-right return first, or approach the eastern shields through the wider lower corridor?

design.captureConsequence: A chamber capture may release pressure into the shared return without automatically filling the other chamber.
design.counterplay: Use wide separated departure points and the short stub returns; avoid waiting on the spine between active roamers.
design.lesson: Each occupied chamber retains its field, while active roamers can share the connecting reclaimed spine.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers and earn territory in both starting chambers without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A familiar central spine becomes a route to cross deliberately rather than a permanent waiting place.
design.routeDecision: Reclaim the upper side first or divide work between both sides before waking the second roamer?

design.captureConsequence: A successful bridge can neutralize terrain, join foundations and redirect a patrol in the same capture.
design.counterplay: Use broad outside bypasses, choose one patrol at a time, and capture marked field before treating it as return ground.
design.lesson: Known slow, lethal, field-retention and frontier rules combine; the rings do not introduce a new surface.
design.mastery: Connect all three rings and neutralize both marked bridges without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Three broken circuits become one readable reclaimed network through a chosen sequence of cuts.
design.routeDecision: Connect the three rings along the long clear outside, or neutralize the marked bridges to form a shorter return circuit?

design.captureConsequence: Each short connection changes your launch angle without automatically claiming a corner. A later enclosure can neutralize terrain and turn the floating end into a longer return route.
design.counterplay: Shift within the central landing before departing toward either rail. Read the locked column, use the hooked tip as a nearer western return, and enclose lethal corners from outside.
design.lesson: The west hook is return ground that redirects the keeper; the east rail floats short of the border. Connecting a rail is a foothold, not a free quadrant.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal corners and connect all three foundations without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The first rail connection leaves the picture contested; steering around its end turns the next return into a meaningful enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Link the hooked west rail or floating east rail first, then choose a return around its end to enclose a dangerous corner?

design.captureConsequence: A bridge may secure only its line while keepers occupy both sides. The new link still gives both craft a shorter return.
design.counterplay: Watch the two keepers; cover different approaches and close onto reclaimed ground or meet both moving heads.
design.lesson: Both craft can build a shared route network from separate foundations.
design.mastery: Both craft contribute a closure before the shared clear, without a knockdown.
design.memorableMoment: Two isolated starting islands become a shared launch corridor.
design.routeDecision: Connect the islands together, or establish opposite return routes first?

design.captureConsequence: Anchor order changes which established connections can be relied upon during later captures.
design.counterplay: Use broad cross arms to change departure direction and avoid following the frontier patrol into a narrow return.
design.lesson: Two captured anchors can protect different connections; five foundations are return choices, not five mandatory chores.
design.mastery: Capture both anchors before reaching three quarters of the earned target, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Two protected routes support a larger capture without requiring every island to be visited.
design.routeDecision: Bank the western connection first, or secure the eastern anchor while keeping a cross-shaped landing between both eroders?

design.captureConsequence: A rewarding capture can create both new return ground and a new threat on that ground.
design.counterplay: Use the wide landing and the warning to move away; plan the next departure before waking the roamer.
design.lesson: A dormant roamer does not retain field. Reclaiming its full body starts a warning, then it moves and threatens reclaimed ground.
design.mastery: Activate the roamer and complete another closure without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The picture opens around a sleeper that warns before it begins moving.
design.routeDecision: Enclose the dormant roamer early and leave by a broad return, or keep its pocket unclaimed while opening the other side?

design.captureConsequence: The required capture banks a stable return connection instead of merely adding a completion checkbox.
design.counterplay: Connect the anchor to useful reclaimed ground before the next enclosure; other earned cells remain vulnerable.
design.lesson: A captured required objective protects its cell and one deterministic reclaimed path to a permanent foundation or outer rail.
design.mastery: Capture the anchor before reaching half of the earned coverage target, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One protected connection survives while neighboring earned frontier remains erodible.
design.routeDecision: Capture the crossing anchor before expanding farther, or use the lower permanent lane to approach from the opposite side?

design.captureConsequence: Relay corners stay permanent while erosion can restore a marked inner spoke. Trail impacts still disappear when a valid closure secures the trail.
design.counterplay: Enclose the two lethal patches before crossing them. The optional speed pickup sits on a wide straight return, away from mandatory precision turns.
design.lesson: This optional combination uses only known roles. The protected circuit and earned spokes have different erosion consequences; neither changes the capture contract.
design.mastery: Traverse both opened corners and neutralize both lethal patches before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: Two missing corners become a complete durable circuit around a changing interior.
design.routeDecision: Complete the protected outer circuit through relay corners, or use the shorter marked center while field threats remain on opposite sides?

design.captureConsequence: Each captured trigger removes a different return detour; opening never performs a second hidden flood.
design.counterplay: Read the inner keeper before a short closure and keep the broad lower opening as an alternative to the gated route.
design.lesson: The field keeper, not a closed gate, retains each chamber. Numbered links change player routes without moving that keeper into another region.
design.mastery: Open the lower connector first and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The inner link opens while the neighbouring keeper remains in exactly the same field component.
design.routeDecision: Open the cross-ring link before taking the inner trigger, or use the open lower approach and preserve the shorter return for later?

design.captureConsequence: A neutralized band changes route efficiency without changing actor movement speeds.
design.counterplay: The central foundation is a permanent return. Keep the exposed part short; capture neutralizes terrain but merely crossing it does not.
design.lesson: Use known terrain rules while planning an impact escape. There is no new mandatory rule in this arc.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal crossbars and close a cut with an active impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A hazardous crossbar becomes the return surface for the next enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Capture a dangerous crossbar from its clear side, or take a shorter slow-band crossing to open another approach?

design.captureConsequence: The first bridge changes return distance while the outer route remains fixed.
design.counterplay: Both landings offer return choices without needing the pickup.
design.lesson: Touch the optional life pickup on reclaimed ground; enclosing it is not collection.
design.mastery: Use both landings before clearing.
design.memorableMoment: A deliberate detour across the landing earns a visible recovery bonus.
design.routeDecision: Use the long landing to wait out a patrol pass, or bridge to the shorter far landing?

design.captureConsequence: A line-only connection can leave both occupied regions in play while still adding a shared bank that shortens the partner’s next exposure.
design.counterplay: Assign the Interceptor to the longer bridge and the Disruptor to the keeper nearest the receiving island. Bank on reclaimed ground only; walls never become returns.
design.lesson: The Interceptor protects the exposed island connection while the Disruptor controls its keeper window. Either completed link becomes a shorter launch point for the partner.
design.mastery: Connect both intermediate islands to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: An offset chain of four islands becomes one shared route network.
design.routeDecision: Take separate stepping stones, or connect across the centre before spreading out?

design.captureConsequence: An enclosure neutralizes the bank immediately, but route resilience depends on which foundations you connect.
design.counterplay: Follow the separate lane and erosion warnings. Repair a cooled bank only when it preserves the shorter route; otherwise use the permanent landing loop so isolated loss never becomes mandatory cleanup.
design.lesson: Lanes and erosion use separate warnings. Foundations never erode; reclaimed hazards can reactivate if earned territory reopens.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal banks, connect all four foundations and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A permanent alternate return remains available when an earned frontier is marked for erosion.
design.routeDecision: Use an earned shortcut across a cooled bank or connect permanent landings before erosion can reopen that route?

design.captureConsequence: Each connection removes a local speed effect and gives a new departure instead of opening an automatic chain of captures.
design.counterplay: Use the central platform to change direction without exposure; the unmarked lower approaches remain usable in either direction.
design.lesson: An interrupted line of landing platforms is not one continuous return. Check the next reclaimed segment before leaving.
design.mastery: Visit both side platforms after connecting them and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A long sideways crossing becomes a plain return lane between two platforms.
design.routeDecision: Connect a distant side platform with the arrows or make the shorter northward return before crossing the open lower field?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting the island creates a shorter return route without automatically filling either side.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: A foundation closes a cut inside the board; it is not earned coverage.
design.mastery: Connect the island before enclosing a large region.
design.memorableMoment: The first return lands inside the board.
design.routeDecision: Land on the nearby island or continue around it to the far boundary?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting the island creates a shorter return route without automatically filling either side.

design.mastery: Connect the island before enclosing a large region.
design.memorableMoment: The first return lands inside the board.
design.routeDecision: Land on the nearby island or continue around it to the far boundary?

design.captureConsequence: Outer captures leave a contested middle instead of automatically filling it. Linking the platform creates a shorter second approach.
design.counterplay: Go around the ends of the staggered walls. The centre keeper makes a blind meeting risky; close onto the platform before changing sides.
design.lesson: Complementary approaches can turn a long winding return into a common launch platform.
design.mastery: Both craft visit the centre platform after it is connected to the perimeter and each closes a cut, without knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Both craft arrive at one middle platform from opposite ends of the switchback.
design.routeDecision: Bank the outer pockets first, or approach the shared middle platform from opposite wall tips?

design.captureConsequence: A connection shortens your return but can also enlarge a roamer’s movement domain.
design.counterplay: The near sleeper wakes behind your first return. Leave its narrow connection for the broad berth; choose when to connect the far sleeper’s separate network.

design.routeDecision: Connect the near sleeper’s corridor now, or establish a side return before joining the far berths?

design.captureConsequence: The western shield joins the upper landing to the inner transfer pad with non-scoring reclaimed connectors.
design.counterplay: Leave space around each baffle end before committing. Capturing the roamer changes pressure on reclaimed returns, not the Sentinel retaining rule.
design.lesson: Separated returns make the opened corner a repositioning route; shield order stays voluntary and the core rules do not change.
design.mastery: Traverse the opened corner before capturing the final shield, then clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A broken transfer corner becomes a walkable alternative to the outer detour.
design.routeDecision: Open the western transfer corner first, or take the long outer approach to a receiver beyond the baffles?

design.captureConsequence: A useful connection can shorten the next cut without making every cell in that connection permanent.
design.counterplay: Keep the central island as a reserve; neutralize the slow approach by enclosure before relying on it.
design.lesson: Isolated foundations provide dependable landings even when the earned links between them are vulnerable.
design.mastery: Join all three foundations and repair eroded ground without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One return link breaks while the island itself remains available.
design.routeDecision: Join the near island through the slowing approach, or open the wider clear side and retain a second return?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing either anchor both protects its cell and opens a non-scoring connector. Earned side shortcuts remain vulnerable to warned erosion.
design.counterplay: Keep the live trail short and bank an anchor connector before repairing earned ground. If a remote cell reopens, use the protected return for the next closure instead of abandoning the route to chase it.
design.lesson: A territory repair and a trail-impact closure race are familiar but different decisions. Permanent foundations, opened connectors and captured objective anchors protect the planned return.
design.mastery: Traverse both opened connectors before clearing without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: An opened T-shaped return stays intact while a nearby earned edge is reopened.
design.routeDecision: Open the upper protected link first, or invest in the lower anchor while the keeper and eroder occupy different corridors?

design.captureConsequence: Corner enclosures establish approaches without automatically emptying the central depot. Inner field keepers retain that territory; reclaimed roamers do not retain field. A timed pickup remains optional and must be touched.
design.counterplay: The two field keepers travel vertically beside the inner shelves. Watch the crossing before extending toward a platform; the outer bays remain useful return approaches. Reclaiming a rover bay can threaten those approaches, so preserve a second exit.
design.lesson: Speed belongs to its collector; enemy pressure and reclaimed return routes remain a shared responsibility.
design.mastery: Take a timed pickup while your partner is cutting, activate both roamers, and clear with returns from both pilots and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Both pilots establish opposite platform connections, then choose different crossings as the inner keepers and reclaimed-ground roamers change the useful return routes.
design.routeDecision: Bank a corner approach, connect an upper or lower platform across a keeper lane, or take an optional speed window for the next connection?

design.captureConsequence: Neutralizing an outer thread changes the efficient approach for both pilots; connecting the middle platform turns that safer approach into a shared bank.
design.counterplay: Use Disruptor Support to control the central keeper while the first connection is exposed, then use Interceptor Support when the partner crosses on the new return. Walls remain blockers, never banks.
design.lesson: One pilot can neutralize a thread and establish the middle return while the other specialist protects the exposed crossing that follows.
design.mastery: Neutralize every material patch and connect the middle platform to the perimeter, with closures from both craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Two winding approaches become one short route through the reclaimed middle.
design.routeDecision: Weave around opposite wall tips to bank the middle, or clear one material lane and share that approach?

design.captureConsequence: The captured part loses its arrows and becomes ordinary reclaimed movement, so the return trip uses a different route budget.
design.counterplay: Read the far landing before accelerating. The wide marked approach has no required turn at its end; the next direction stays your choice.
design.lesson: Arrows change craft speed only while moving on unclaimed cells: faster with, slower against, unchanged across. They never push a stopped craft.
design.mastery: Reclaim both marked fields completely and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The marked center route disappears behind a stopped craft while neighboring arrows remain.
design.routeDecision: Take the marked run to the central landing, or a shorter unmarked slice near the western platform?

design.captureConsequence: A near-shield capture extends the central return without changing earned coverage. The final explicit release reveals the remaining picture and ends the core route.
design.counterplay: Keep room around the active frontier and leave a western escape for the awakened roamer. Captured shields and opened dock survive life recovery; the last release still needs the advertised opening.
design.lesson: The final core uses the same shield count, warning, transition and release rule already learned. The branching returns ask for a route order, not a new boss control.
design.mastery: Connect and visit a wing platform on each side before releasing the core without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: A connected homeward dock supports the last enclosure, followed by a voluntary choice of Remix, mastery, replay or exit.
design.routeDecision: Connect the western wing to preserve an escape first, or disable the near shield to extend the permanent release dock?

design.captureConsequence: A connection makes a new return surface, not a guaranteed large reveal. The next enclosure depends on which side each keeper occupies.
design.counterplay: Read the western keeper before enclosing the near shore and the eastern keeper before the long crossing. Reposition on the island to choose an upper or lower departure.
design.lesson: An interior outpost offers several departures. Keepers on opposite sides can retain both regions after a cut; a small bridge can still create useful return angles.
design.mastery: Reach two different perimeter sides.
design.memorableMoment: A line-only bridge becomes the launch point for a smaller enclosure around the keeper on that shore.
design.routeDecision: Establish the short western bridge beside its keeper, or time the longer eastern return before choosing the next enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: A secured connection shelters the craft from the lane, while the stationary emitter continues retaining its field region.
design.counterplay: Watch the marked row and close on the landing before the attack. Start the next crossing after the active lane clears.
design.lesson: A lane locks to your row, warns, then fires. Moving the craft out is not enough if the unfinished trail still crosses it.
design.mastery: Clear without a life loss after closing a cut whose exposed trail crossed a warning lane.
design.memorableMoment: The first cut closes after the lock appears and before the lane fires.
design.routeDecision: Close on the landing during the warning, or carry a longer exposed trail toward the far border?

design.captureConsequence: Connection order changes frontier pressure; only the two field keepers retain regions.
design.counterplay: Keep an interior retreat while choosing which optional bonus detour is worth its exposure.
design.lesson: Combine known keeper, outer-patrol and frontier-patrol rules; no new mandatory mechanic.
design.mastery: Connect all three foundations without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same new bridge is a useful return and a possible future patrol edge.
design.routeDecision: Link the nearer spine first or approach the far island before its frontier patrol comes around?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. The adapted actor still retains its occupied field region, while the existing wall, foundation and patrol rules remain unchanged.
design.counterplay: Depart away from the frontier patrol, break the pursuer’s sight with a wall segment, and commit only after choosing a reachable return.
design.lesson: The open pysanka-inspired sections provide sight screens, not secret capture chambers; only real landings close the cut.
design.mastery: Use both a wall-screened departure and a short pursued closure.
design.memorableMoment: The decorative oval becomes useful cover while the frontier continues around the changing boundary.
design.routeDecision: Leave the spindle through the near oval opening, or use the segmented wall as a sight screen before reaching the far return?

design.captureConsequence: An outer connection creates new launch angles but cannot claim the occupied courtyard. An inward capture creates shorter interior returns without clearing the outside for free.
design.counterplay: Watch the keeper in the field you are entering. Move along reclaimed ring ground to shorten the exposed route, and close before a keeper reaches your line.
design.lesson: The ring separates two keeper-held fields. Its outer edge offers short returns; its inner edge supports larger enclosures. Both fields matter to the clear.
design.mastery: Complete an inward cut and an outward cut.
design.memorableMoment: A short outer bridge changes the next launch, then an inward enclosure reveals the courtyard at a different scale.
design.routeDecision: Take the short outer bridge first, or move along the ring to choose an inward enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: Each chamber remains until its own retaining actors are isolated; there is no unexplained remote fill.
design.counterplay: Follow the change in boundary height before committing. Slice across each chamber toward the nearer part of the dogleg.
design.lesson: The two chambers retain independently; the permanent dogleg closes cuts but does not itself earn coverage.
design.mastery: Make a closure in both starting chambers and neutralize the lower lethal pocket without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One stepped return gives two different useful closure heights.
design.routeDecision: Work the shallow upper chamber first, or use the dogleg to reach the deeper lower chamber?

design.captureConsequence: Connection order changes the fastest return route and which marked channel can be neutralized next.
design.counterplay: The upper and lower clear approaches remain available; the freeze detour is optional.
design.lesson: Combine known terrain and patrol rules; no new mandatory mechanic is introduced.
design.mastery: Link all three refuges without collecting the optional freeze.
design.memorableMoment: Three separated refuges become a route network through two distinct kinds of field.
design.routeDecision: Link the near and central refuges through slow ground, or loop around the marked channel to the far landing?

design.captureConsequence: A connection changes the next launch angle without automatically filling the other occupied side. Enclosing the hot pocket makes a new approach usable.
design.counterplay: Use the central platform to change direction. The west rail opens the slow-side approach; the east rail offers a return beneath the hot pocket. Keep a real return beyond every bend.
design.lesson: The lower elbow keeps a field keeper on the west approach. Rails close cuts; the elbow wall does not. Read the locked row before choosing which rail to join.
design.mastery: Join all three foundations and neutralize the lethal pocket without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Two staggered rails stay useful for different reasons after the first long connector leaves both enemy-held sides contested.
design.routeDecision: Connect the west rail for an approach around the elbow, or establish the east rail and neutralize its hot pocket first?

design.captureConsequence: Opposite captures can build a shared central corridor. A line-only closure still supplies a return route while occupied regions stay unclaimed.
design.counterplay: The west spine offers several returns; the east refuge has clear upper and lower bypasses. Watch both keepers before a long vertical cut.
design.lesson: A partner can neutralize material for both craft; the lethal bed must be enclosed before either craft crosses it.
design.mastery: Neutralize both material beds with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: One partner opens the marked crossing while the other turns a slow approach into ordinary shared ground.
design.routeDecision: Split the outer bypasses to enclose both material beds, or first link a shared return through the slow approach?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting an off-axis landing gives a shorter approach through a different side of the motif.
design.counterplay: Inspect both open sides before leaving. Each landing offers several departures; a wall touch is not a return.
design.lesson: The ornament is made of walls: only the contrasting reclaimed landings can close a cut.
design.mastery: Connect both far landings before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: Two apparent decorative diamonds become useful choices of crossing direction.
design.routeDecision: Thread an opening in a stepped diamond, or take the longer outer route to the next landing?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing a relay joins its store to the spine and gives a shorter later departure without mandatory corridor cleanup.
design.counterplay: Use the open side of each store to enclose a trigger instead of tracing every bend of the structure.
design.lesson: A shortcut changes return distance, not the meaning of the surrounding open field. Broad exits remain available before either relay.
design.mastery: Open both shortcuts within two consecutive captures and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: An apparently winding route becomes a direct permanent connection after one deliberate enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Break the western inward route at the top or the eastern route at the bottom before moving across the central spine?

design.captureConsequence: The west connector opens approaches on both sides of the baffles, while occupied field still remains unclaimed. Each new frontier changes the patrol route.
design.counterplay: Keep a real landing at the end of the cut. Cross the open aisle during a rest window, or turn around a baffle end after reading the marked column.
design.lesson: A locked column threatens the exposed trail. A west landing and a northern landing offer different returns; baffles are walls, never return surfaces.
design.mastery: Connect all three foundations and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A completed westward connector remains usable through the column attack, then offers a different approach around the upper baffle.
design.routeDecision: Connect the west landing through the open aisle, or establish the northern return before working around the baffle ends?

design.captureConsequence: Neutralized vertical links simplify later travel, but the stationary emitter still retains field and follows the same attack schedule.
design.counterplay: Stage on a broad platform; wait out the lower lane warning without drawing, then choose a return above it or through its recovery.
design.lesson: Arrow speed changes travel time, not attack warnings or enemy speed. Read the full route and the next landing before using a window.
design.mastery: Reclaim the east and west marked links and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Opposing long lanes stop being asymmetric after they are reclaimed.
design.routeDecision: Use the short alternating vertical links or make a wider unmarked capture during a visible lane-emitter recovery?

design.captureConsequence: Enclosing the band neutralizes its slowing effect and creates a faster future approach.
design.counterplay: The first crossing leads to a broad return; inspect the keeper before choosing the exposed shortcut.
design.lesson: Paired dashes slow the craft only while this ground is unclaimed. Enemies keep their catalog speed.
design.mastery: Neutralize the whole slow band without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A route that was slow becomes ordinary reclaimed ground after the enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Cross the short slow band to reach the island, or take the longer clear approach around it?

design.captureConsequence: A completed orchard enclosure removes its material penalty and opens that chamber as a staging route for the partner’s next cut.
design.counterplay: Let the Interceptor cover the longer lethal-orchard cut and the Disruptor create a keeper window around the slow orchard. Swap spatial jobs through the perimeter when the safer enclosure is on the other side.
design.lesson: The Interceptor protects the exposed orchard enclosure while the Disruptor controls its keeper. Neutralizing either material problem gives both pilots an ordinary full-speed route on that side.
design.mastery: Neutralize both orchards, with each craft closing in its starting chamber and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Different material problems resolve into two connected, ordinary movement areas.
design.routeDecision: Enclose the lethal orchard from outside while the other craft crosses the slow bay, or swap roles around the perimeter?

design.captureConsequence: Each chamber remains until its own retaining actors are isolated; there is no unexplained remote fill.
design.counterplay: Follow the change in boundary height before committing. Slice across each chamber toward the nearer part of the dogleg.
design.lesson: The two chambers retain independently; the permanent dogleg closes cuts but does not itself earn coverage.
design.mastery: Make a closure in both starting chambers and neutralize the lower lethal pocket without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One stepped return gives two different useful closure heights.
design.routeDecision: Work the shallow upper chamber first, or use the dogleg to reach the deeper lower chamber?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. Field-retaining enemies still determine which regions remain unclaimed, and the existing terrain or patrol consequences remain active.
design.counterplay: Keep the northern landing in reserve. Close before the committed approach arrives, or put reclaimed ground or a wall between the pursuer and the next exposed trail.
design.lesson: The pursuer warns, locks one observed point on the unfinished trail, and commits for a finite route. It never retargets invisibly during that commitment.
design.mastery: Close a cut with an active travelling impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A short landing closure cancels a visibly committed pursuit before the lower bay asks for a different route.
design.routeDecision: Close at the nearby northern landing when pursuit locks, or risk the longer lower enclosure while the committed route remains visible?

design.captureConsequence: Material neutralization and roamer activation can occur in the same enclosure; both partners must read the changed board.
design.counterplay: Use the side spines to change departure heights. Enclose crosses before entering them and leave space around the courtyard when a roamer wakes.
design.lesson: Removing a terrain hazard does not make every reclaimed route free of enemies.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers and connect the courtyard to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: A dangerous garden becomes passable just as the tracked bodies make the surrounding ground busy.
design.routeDecision: Neutralize the upper hazard before linking the courtyard, or establish the lower slow-field approach while the partner prepares a different exit?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing one bay does not remove the keeper from the other.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: A starting return lane can separate two independently retained regions.
design.mastery: Earn territory on both sides without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same central lane supports two different enclosure rhythms.
design.routeDecision: Work one bay to completion or alternate sides to follow the safer keeper positions?

design.captureConsequence: The required capture banks a stable return connection instead of merely adding a completion checkbox.
design.counterplay: Connect the anchor to useful reclaimed ground before the next enclosure; other earned cells remain vulnerable.
design.lesson: A captured required objective protects its cell and one deterministic reclaimed path to a permanent foundation or outer rail.
design.mastery: Capture the anchor before reaching half of the earned coverage target, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One protected connection survives while neighboring earned frontier remains erodible.
design.routeDecision: Capture the crossing anchor before expanding farther, or use the lower permanent lane to approach from the opposite side?

design.captureConsequence: A new return reshapes the frontier and may move its patrol toward your next departure.
design.counterplay: Depart from the side away from the frontier patrol and choose a return before entering an opening.
design.lesson: This egg-decoration-inspired outline stays open; walls cannot create a secretly empty sealed chamber.
design.mastery: Use one side opening and one stepped end opening.
design.memorableMoment: An inward enclosure changes which opening is useful on the next outward cut.
design.routeDecision: Leave the central spindle through a side opening, or reach past the segmented oval end?

design.captureConsequence: Reconnecting the spine creates a useful route that both active roamers may also use.
design.counterplay: Use broad gaps and distinct upper/lower returns, neutralize marked pockets by enclosure and leave a fresh departure ready.
design.lesson: Combine known retention, return-ground, terrain and threat-domain rules; no new mandatory mechanic.
design.mastery: Join the three spine segments and activate both roamers without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: An apparently broken return network becomes useful only after choosing how to keep it escapable.
design.routeDecision: Reconnect the broken spine, or first establish a vertical escape before the two sleepers gain access to it?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. The adapted actor still retains its occupied field region, while the existing wall, foundation and patrol rules remain unchanged.
design.counterplay: Choose two reachable pads, wait for the aim point, then turn around the central component wall toward the pad the interceptor did not target.
design.lesson: Interception predicts only the observed heading. The four motor-like pads provide deliberate alternatives after the visible lock.
design.mastery: Feint after a lock and connect all four pads without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A propeller-like four-pad layout turns one warned attack into a satisfying mid-route feint.
design.routeDecision: Keep the direct motor-pad heading after the target locks, or turn toward an adjacent pad and leave the committed intercept behind?

design.captureConsequence: A successful enclosure turns the dangerous center into a new traversable return surface.
design.counterplay: The first return and broad outside approaches avoid the marked bed entirely.
design.lesson: Framed crosses harm the craft on unclaimed field. Capturing that field neutralizes the hazard.
design.mastery: Neutralize the whole central bed without visiting the far landing first.
design.memorableMoment: The crossed warning disappears from earned ground without changing the underlying map rule.
design.routeDecision: Enclose the marked central bed before crossing, or keep a longer clear path around it?

design.captureConsequence: Each shore connection changes which branch end is a useful next departure; a connection between occupied regions may earn only its trail.
design.counterplay: Keep a second landing within reach and read the keeper beyond the next branch. The broad outer route is an alternative when the central passage is contested.
design.lesson: The bank ornaments are walls, not shore returns. Separate reclaimed platforms close cuts; the field keepers retain their ordinary field regions.
design.mastery: Connect both shores using a central passage and an outer-bank approach before clearing without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A small central connection opens a new crossing angle, while the far bank still needs a differently shaped enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Link the central landing through the gap between branching banks, or take a wider shore-to-shore crossing around a flower-and-bird silhouette?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing removes live impacts and neutralizes terrain, but may activate a new ground threat without disabling either emitter.
design.counterplay: Shorten the live trail before the marked cross fires and leave an exit on reclaimed ground before capturing the roamer.
design.lesson: Combine known lane, impact and reclaimed-ground threats. A travelling spark has grace; an active lane striking the trail does not.
design.mastery: Clear without a life loss after closing an active-impact cut while the roamer was already active.
design.memorableMoment: A timely closure extinguishes a moving impact while the new ground still offers an escape from the roamer.
design.routeDecision: Spend the rest window linking another refuge, or close a smaller cut and preserve a corridor before the roamer wakes?

design.captureConsequence: A line-only link can still shorten both routes while occupied regions remain unclaimed.
design.counterplay: The upper and lower keepers leave different departure windows. Use the intermediate islands to shorten exposure; a wall is never a return.
design.lesson: A hit on either unfinished Team line sends visible fronts along that player’s current cut. Bank it before the craft-bound front arrives.
design.mastery: Connect both intermediate islands to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: An offset chain of four islands becomes one shared route network.
design.routeDecision: Take separate stepping stones, or connect across the centre before spreading out?

design.captureConsequence: A landing connection improves your next escape without clearing the other occupied bay. Neither bay alone reaches the coverage target.
design.counterplay: The northern landing offers a short return. Watch every field enemy before extending your trail; close before its impact reaches you. Use the center deck to change bays, and never mistake a wall for a return.
design.lesson: Every field enemy sends a travelling impact when it strikes an unfinished trail; each occupied bay retains its own field.
design.mastery: Close a cut with an active travelling impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A small landing return extinguishes an impact; the lower bay then asks for a different enclosure around its baffles.
design.routeDecision: Practice a short northern landing return, or work around the lower baffles for a larger enclosure between two keepers?

design.captureConsequence: A useful connection can shorten the next cut without making every cell in that connection permanent.
design.counterplay: Keep the central island as a reserve; neutralize the slow approach by enclosure before relying on it.
design.lesson: Isolated foundations provide dependable landings even when the earned links between them are vulnerable.
design.mastery: Join all three foundations and repair eroded ground without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One return link breaks while the island itself remains available.
design.routeDecision: Join the near island through the slowing approach, or open the wider clear side and retain a second return?

design.captureConsequence: The first receiver advances the visible shield count while the original attack cadence continues. Only the final shield cancels that lane and starts the transition.
design.counterplay: The broken central return leaves the whole field connected initially. Both receivers lie inside the retained chamber; outer captures do not collect them. Keep the northward opening available and stay clear of the core body.
design.lesson: Every listed shield must be captured; one relay does not expose the core. Their display order does not force a route order.
design.mastery: Capture the eastern shield before the western shield, in separate closures, and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Two opposing receiver sites share one Sentinel without a free half-board reveal.
design.routeDecision: Approach the western receiver around the core, or the eastern receiver first, while preserving the five-cell return opening?

design.captureConsequence: The south bridge becomes permanent reclaimed ground without awarding coverage or releasing either field keeper.
design.counterplay: Close on the existing platform first. The opened bridge then reaches a second landing without another exposed crossing.
design.lesson: Capture the numbered trigger to open its matching connector. A closed crossbar blocks a cut; an opened connector closes it.
design.mastery: Use the opened bridge to reach the lower landing and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: One short closure visibly joins two separated landings before the next route begins.
design.routeDecision: Land through the visible relay to establish a permanent southward shortcut, or keep using the longer outside return?

design.captureConsequence: The marked shortcut becomes ordinary-speed reclaimed ground. The roamer may now use it too, so the outer stepping platforms retain their value.
design.counterplay: The first broad arrow has a clear landing and no forced turn. Leave the locked column before it fires; retain a second departure when reclaiming the roamer.
design.lesson: A direct arrow route can be efficient without being the best return after a capture. The locked lane and awakened ground domain remain separately readable.
design.mastery: Connect and visit the upper and lower stepping platforms before clearing without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The fastest outward route turns into contested reclaimed ground, making the quieter stepping return useful.
design.routeDecision: Use the fast long crossing toward the middle landing, or claim the upper stepping platform before awakening the ground roamer?

design.captureConsequence: The slow-bed closure makes a broad western return; the upper closure creates a narrow eastern departure without neutralizing the hot bed.
design.counterplay: The western line is direct but slow. The upper branch avoids the lethal bed, costs more distance, and exposes a different frontier timing.
design.lesson: The non-crossing branches supply safe staging while the existing slow and lethal beds retain their exact rules and cells.
design.mastery: Close from both branch approaches without entering the lethal bed or losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A flowing, non-crossing branch route lets the player choose a slow garden bed or an ambitious arc above heat.
design.routeDecision: Cross the western slow bed directly from the side branch, or climb the safe stem and arc above the eastern hot bed for a faster but longer enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: A connection around a branch creates a shorter departure, not a free district clear. Neutralizing the eastern hazard creates usable ground until erosion restores its underlying danger; foundations stay protected.
design.counterplay: Inspect the short wall beside the center start, then choose an opening above or below it. Compare the two western branch ends with the eastern middle gap; use the spine when an earned approach erodes.
design.lesson: The alternating kilim-inspired branches are walls, not returns. Both districts retain an eroder and a keeper; the permanent center spine still lets you change districts without losing that refuge.
design.mastery: Close a cut in each district, use a branch end and the eastern middle gap, and neutralize the eastern hazard without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The open flower on one side offers a middle mouth while the longer branch on the other demands a choice of ends.
design.routeDecision: Work around the western branch ends to bank the small island, or pass the eastern flower gap toward its taller return and lethal pocket?

design.captureConsequence: Each short connection changes your launch angle without automatically claiming a corner. A later enclosure can neutralize terrain and turn the floating end into a longer return route.
design.counterplay: Shift within the central landing before departing toward either rail. Read the locked column, use the hooked tip as a nearer western return, and enclose lethal corners from outside.
design.lesson: The west hook is return ground that redirects the keeper; the east rail floats short of the border. Connecting a rail is a foothold, not a free quadrant.
design.mastery: Neutralize both lethal corners and connect all three foundations without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The first rail connection leaves the picture contested; steering around its end turns the next return into a meaningful enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Link the hooked west rail or floating east rail first, then choose a return around its end to enclose a dangerous corner?

design.captureConsequence: An earned connection can extend both the craft’s return network and the awakened rover’s movement domain; the branch walls stay impassable.
design.counterplay: Choose a departure and a second work mat before enclosing the sleeper. Use the unequal branch ends to keep a parallel escape rather than trapping yourself in one earned aisle.
design.lesson: Branching work-mat obstacles are walls, not reclaimed trunks. Capturing the sleeping rover’s field activates pressure on reclaimed ground after its warning.
design.mastery: Wake the rover and then use three different work mats, including an outer escape, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The central shortcut becomes contested, making the previously established outer mat immediately useful.
design.routeDecision: Reclaim the aisle between staggered branches and wake the rover, or connect an outer work mat first so a parallel escape survives activation?

design.captureConsequence: The west connector opens approaches on both sides of the baffles, while occupied field still remains unclaimed. Each new frontier changes the patrol route.
design.counterplay: Keep a real landing at the end of the cut. Cross the open aisle during a rest window, or turn around a baffle end after reading the marked column.
design.lesson: A locked column threatens the exposed trail. A west landing and a northern landing offer different returns; baffles are walls, never return surfaces.
design.mastery: Connect all three foundations and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A completed westward connector remains usable through the column attack, then offers a different approach around the upper baffle.
design.routeDecision: Connect the west landing through the open aisle, or establish the northern return before working around the baffle ends?

design.captureConsequence: Joining the upper island changes the frontier and shortens later returns. The right-hand branch still separates an inner approach from the outer shoulder; a wall impact cannot substitute for either landing.
design.counterplay: Inspect the branch immediately above reclaimed home ground. Leave around its left or right tip, watch the impact carrier before the upper turn, and keep an exterior return available when the frontier pressures the small island.
design.lesson: The Petrykivka-inspired noncrossing branches block the direct upward link but never close cuts. Choose which real landing will receive the cut before leaving the home platform.
design.mastery: Connect both foundations, use an inner fork and an exterior branch approach, and close a cut with an active impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A short fork connects the upper return, while the longer outer branch keeps a visibly different fallback route around the same two landings.
design.routeDecision: Turn through the short split below the upper island, or work around a longer branch while keeping the broad home landing as your fallback?

design.captureConsequence: A mouth closure may secure only the connecting line; an outside enclosure can instead move patrol pressure.
design.counterplay: Use the broad ring as a return; compare the inner keeper, lower approach keeper and outer contour before crossing.
design.lesson: Closing a ring does not fill an occupied center. The keeper, not the visible loop, determines retained field.
design.mastery: Earn a closure through the ring mouth and connect the ring to the perimeter without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A visually closed ring can still contain unclaimed ground, with its retaining enemy plainly visible.
design.routeDecision: Close the mouth around the inner keeper first, or grow an outside return while the ring remains open?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting the posts creates an inner escape corridor, while capturing the roamer changes pressure on the outer loop.
design.counterplay: Preserve two exits before activating the roamer. Broad upper and lower approaches bypass the middle arrow penalty.
design.lesson: A return loop supports movement but may become roamer territory. Marked speed never makes reclaimed ground universally safe.
design.mastery: Visit both interior posts after connecting them and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A slow middle gap becomes a direct escape after its enclosing cut.
design.routeDecision: Cross the shorter inner posts, including an against-arrow gap, or reposition along the long reclaimed U before taking the outer approach?

design.captureConsequence: A pad connection creates a return beyond a frame arm; retaining enemies still determine which side fills.
