design.counterplay: Use an adjacent pad for a short closure, observe the keepers across all three aisles, and depart behind the outer patrol.
design.lesson: The four reclaimed pads are real return surfaces; the central component is an impassable wall.
design.mastery: Connect all four pads without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The open frame arms turn four pads into a choice of changing approach directions.
design.routeDecision: Connect an offset motor pad through the inner aisle, or circle a frame arm for a wider enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: The western shield joins the upper landing to the inner transfer pad with non-scoring reclaimed connectors.
design.counterplay: Leave space around each baffle end before committing. Capturing the roamer changes pressure on reclaimed returns, not the Sentinel retaining rule.
design.lesson: Separated returns make the opened corner a repositioning route; shield order stays voluntary and the core rules do not change.
design.mastery: Traverse the opened corner before capturing the final shield, then clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A broken transfer corner becomes a walkable alternative to the outer detour.
design.routeDecision: Open the western transfer corner first, or take the long outer approach to a receiver beyond the baffles?

design.captureConsequence: A completed chamber contributes earned territory without automatically clearing the other occupied chambers.
design.counterplay: Reposition along the broad cross; the four field keepers cannot leave their starting chambers without a field connection.
design.lesson: Each occupied chamber retains its own field. Permanent cross lanes provide returns but do not earn coverage.
design.mastery: Make captures in three different starting chambers without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same central crossing lets the player choose the order of unequal spatial problems.
design.routeDecision: Start with a small near quadrant, or use the spacious cross to tackle the larger region while its keeper is distant?

design.captureConsequence: A larger capture may disable several shields together, but it also enlarges the reclaimed area available to the roamer and redirects the frontier patrol.
design.counterplay: Read the two moving domains before making a long cut. The broad middle and outer platforms offer repositioning without forcing precision turns under acceleration.
design.lesson: Four shield sites ask for an objective order and a return plan; the boss warning, movement and release rules remain unchanged.
design.mastery: Capture the four shields in four separate closures and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The last of four shield sites disappears and the central route becomes the launch point for the release cut.
design.routeDecision: Disable several shields with one ambitious enclosure, or secure separate return platforms while controlling the roamer and changing frontier?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. Field-retaining enemies still determine which regions remain unclaimed, and the existing terrain or patrol consequences remain active.
design.counterplay: Shape the frontier away from both exits, provoke a readable lock, then close at the return the pursuer did not commit toward.
design.lesson: A second return is useful only when it is reachable before the finite pursuit commitment reaches the exposed trail.
design.mastery: Connect both foundations and close a cut with an active impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The unused landing turns a pressured cut into a safe alternate closure and redirects the frontier patrol.
design.routeDecision: Link the upper landing before provoking pursuit, or preserve two separate returns and choose one after the target locks?

design.captureConsequence: The south bridge becomes permanent reclaimed ground without awarding coverage or releasing either field keeper.
design.counterplay: Close on the existing platform first. The opened bridge then reaches a second landing without another exposed crossing.
design.lesson: Capture the numbered trigger to open its matching connector. A closed crossbar blocks a cut; an opened connector closes it.
design.mastery: Use the opened bridge to reach the lower landing and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: One short closure visibly joins two separated landings before the next route begins.
design.routeDecision: Land through the visible relay to establish a permanent southward shortcut, or keep using the longer outside return?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting the posts creates an inner escape corridor, while capturing the roamer changes pressure on the outer loop.
design.counterplay: Preserve two exits before activating the roamer. Broad upper and lower approaches bypass the middle arrow penalty.
design.lesson: A return loop supports movement but may become roamer territory. Marked speed never makes reclaimed ground universally safe.
design.mastery: Visit both interior posts after connecting them and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A slow middle gap becomes a direct escape after its enclosing cut.
design.routeDecision: Cross the shorter inner posts, including an against-arrow gap, or reposition along the long reclaimed U before taking the outer approach?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting an island shortens later returns without clearing its occupied district. The permanent center lane never erodes; earned approaches can.
design.counterplay: Use the center spine to switch districts when pressure builds. Walls never close cuts; the islands do. Read both field anchors before a large slice.
design.lesson: Each district contains an eroder and a keeper. A cut between occupied pockets secures only its line; choose the return that improves your next enclosure.
design.mastery: Close a cut in each district and neutralize the eastern hazard without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A modest island connection becomes a new departure around a baffle while the far pocket remains visibly occupied.
design.routeDecision: Bank the short western island return, work around the eastern baffle to reach its taller landing, or risk a broad outer enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: Outer captures leave a contested middle instead of automatically filling it. Linking the platform creates a shorter second approach.
design.counterplay: Go around the ends of the staggered walls. The centre keeper makes a blind meeting risky; close onto the platform before changing sides.
design.lesson: Complementary approaches can turn a long winding return into a common launch platform.
design.mastery: Both craft visit the centre platform after it is connected to the perimeter and each closes a cut, without knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Both craft arrive at one middle platform from opposite ends of the switchback.
design.routeDecision: Bank the outer pockets first, or approach the shared middle platform from opposite wall tips?

design.captureConsequence: Each shore connection offers a shorter next approach around a different breakwater end.
design.counterplay: Keep a second internal landing within reach instead of relying on a single outside-border return.
design.lesson: Shore platforms are real returns; staggered breakwaters and keepers in separated approaches make crossing order matter.
design.mastery: Connect landings on both shores before the final enclosure.
design.memorableMoment: A narrow bridge opens a wide choice of later river crossings.
design.routeDecision: Link the central landing to pass the staggered breakwater, or take the wider outer crossing?

design.captureConsequence: A capture beside the bend changes the next frontier without changing the permanent return or denominator.
design.counterplay: Use the wide central bend to change approach, and neutralize the optional slow patch before a longer crossing.
design.lesson: A connected foundation can separate occupied field regions while frontier and perimeter patrols keep distinct routes.
design.mastery: Earn territory on both sides of the dogleg and neutralize the slow patch without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A route that looks long on the board can be the shorter exposed trail.
design.routeDecision: Enclose beside the short bend, or use the long dogleg to leave the patrol on the opposite side?

design.captureConsequence: A short passage connection can make the far band easier to approach without changing patrol domain.
design.counterplay: Use the internal return strips while the outside patrol passes; keep one passage available for the next cut.
design.lesson: Repeated bands do not repeat the same route: their openings alternate sides.
design.mastery: Close a cut through each of the two inner passages.
design.memorableMoment: A left-to-right crossing becomes a right-to-left problem at the next band.
design.routeDecision: Cross at the staggered inner passage, or circle the end of the textile-like band for a larger enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: A captured spoke becomes ordinary reclaimed movement. An earned corner approach links different windbreaks around the broken arcs, changing the patrol frontier without rotating or covering an arrow with a wall.
design.counterplay: Turn on the central platform before taking a straight boosted spoke. Compare a return against its arrow with the unmarked gap around a ring end; read the frontier before connecting the next windbreak.
design.lesson: The broken concentric composition uses walls only in the unmarked quadrants. All four arrow directions, strengths and broad landings stay fixed; the frontier changes after a capture, not the speed-field rules.
design.mastery: Connect three outer windbreaks and complete an unmarked ring-gap approach without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: An outward fast crossing and an unmarked corner return solve different halves of the same broken-ring route.
design.routeDecision: Take an unchanged fast spoke into a broad windbreak, or thread an unmarked break between carved-ring shoulders to approach another return without opposing its arrow?

design.captureConsequence: A closure changes the contour that the patrol follows; it does not become a field-retaining enemy.
design.counterplay: The first return approaches the broad top of the island, away from the patrol on its left edge.
design.lesson: Unlike the outer patrol, a frontier patrol follows the changing field/reclaimed boundary.
design.mastery: Create a new frontier and depart from a different edge.
design.memorableMoment: The newly reclaimed edge becomes part of the patrol route.
design.routeDecision: Close ahead of the moving frontier patrol, or shape a return on the opposite side of its route?

design.captureConsequence: A larger capture may disable several shields together, but it also enlarges the reclaimed area available to the roamer and redirects the frontier patrol.
design.counterplay: Read the two moving domains before making a long cut. The broad middle and outer platforms offer repositioning without forcing precision turns under acceleration.
design.lesson: Four shield sites ask for an objective order and a return plan; the boss warning, movement and release rules remain unchanged.
design.mastery: Capture the four shields in four separate closures and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The last of four shield sites disappears and the central route becomes the launch point for the release cut.
design.routeDecision: Disable several shields with one ambitious enclosure, or secure separate return platforms while controlling the roamer and changing frontier?

design.captureConsequence: A modest return can establish a new approach around a baffle without erasing the occupied far pocket. Reclaimed routes remain exposed to roamers.
design.counterplay: Keep the centre of the broad spine available. Approach either side of a stub after reading its roamer; walls block movement and never close a cut.
design.lesson: The two roamer lanes warn from the start. Each field chamber has two retaining keepers, so separating occupied pockets may bank only the trail.
design.mastery: Earn territory in both starting chambers and close at both stub returns after the roamers activate, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A fast return lands beside a moving roamer; the next cut leaves from the opposite side of the same stub.
design.routeDecision: Take a broad outer slice, use a stub return around its baffle, or switch chambers before a roamer meets your landing?

design.captureConsequence: Both chambers contribute to the same coverage quota. Neither half alone can supply the required clear.
design.counterplay: The divider blocks movement and never banks a trail. Return to an island or the perimeter; each chamber has a visible keeper.
design.lesson: Each occupied chamber needs its own useful capture; closing one side does not clear the other.
design.mastery: Each craft closes in its starting chamber and connects its island to the perimeter without a knockdown.
design.memorableMoment: Two independent enclosures transform opposite halves of one board.
design.routeDecision: Work opposite chambers in parallel, or travel around the perimeter to help the pressured partner?

design.captureConsequence: Two independently earned connectors turn three landings into a usable cross-board return.
design.counterplay: Choose a visible return before entering the upper field and watch the frontier at the far landing.
design.lesson: Each number is a separate capture link. Opening one connector does not open every gate.
design.mastery: Open the eastern connector before the western connector and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The same upper trigger can be approached from the outer rail or the newly connected middle platform.
design.routeDecision: Open the nearer link to gain a central launch point, or approach the eastern trigger from the outer boundary first?

design.captureConsequence: A modest return can establish a new approach around a baffle without erasing the occupied far pocket. Reclaimed routes remain exposed to roamers.
design.counterplay: Keep the centre of the broad spine available. Approach either side of a stub after reading its roamer; walls block movement and never close a cut.
design.lesson: The two roamer lanes warn from the start. Each field chamber has two retaining keepers, so separating occupied pockets may bank only the trail.
design.mastery: Earn territory in both starting chambers and close at both stub returns after the roamers activate, without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A fast return lands beside a moving roamer; the next cut leaves from the opposite side of the same stub.
design.routeDecision: Take a broad outer slice, use a stub return around its baffle, or switch chambers before a roamer meets your landing?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting the middle landing changes the approach to the rotated motif. Keepers still retain their current field regions, so a useful connection may bank only its trail.
design.counterplay: Use the lower edge of the starting landing for the open mouth, or depart above the shoulder. Read the keeper courses before turning toward the offset return; no pickup is required.
design.lesson: From the starting reclaimed landing, inspect the wall to the right: walls block craft and keepers but never close a cut. Only reclaimed ground is a return; the second diamond opens on a different axis.
design.mastery: Connect both detached landings using a motif mouth and an exterior shoulder approach without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The second stitched diamond cannot be crossed by repeating the first horizontal route.
design.routeDecision: Thread the first diamond mouth to the offset middle landing, or enclose around its upper shoulder before approaching the north-south motif?

design.captureConsequence: The two occupied chambers retain independently. One partner can finish a material job while the other builds the shared coverage.
design.counterplay: The west orchard must be enclosed, never crossed unclaimed. The east orchard is crossable but prolongs exposure; the divider is a wall, not a return.
design.lesson: Equal controls do not mean identical jobs: lethal and slow field call for different approaches.
design.mastery: Neutralize both orchards, with each craft closing in its starting chamber and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Different material problems resolve into two connected, ordinary movement areas.
design.routeDecision: Enclose the lethal orchard from outside while the other craft crosses the slow bay, or swap roles around the perimeter?

design.captureConsequence: Connecting an off-axis landing gives a shorter approach through a different side of the motif.
design.counterplay: Inspect both open sides before leaving. Each landing offers several departures; a wall touch is not a return.
design.lesson: The ornament is made of walls: only the contrasting reclaimed landings can close a cut.
design.mastery: Connect both far landings before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: Two apparent decorative diamonds become useful choices of crossing direction.
design.routeDecision: Thread an opening in a stepped diamond, or take the longer outer route to the next landing?

design.captureConsequence: The near relay opens a permanent non-scoring home dock. Other captures neutralize field only where no keeper remains, and can wake the roamer on reclaimed ground. Captured objectives persist through ordinary recovery.
design.counterplay: Watch both keeper positions before departing; an enemy on each side can leave a line-only capture. Keep an upper or dock return ready before enclosing the ground roamer. The freeze pickup is optional.
design.lesson: The finale combines the familiar enemy-retained capture rule with relay returns and reclaimed-ground pressure. There is no boss shield or release window: enclose the four visible signal objectives and reach the coverage target.
design.mastery: Connect and visit a western wing and either far-eastern platform before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: An opened dock can offer a homeward return after a wide reveal wakes the roamer; choose a return rather than wait for a boss opening.
design.routeDecision: Capture the near relay to open the home dock, or establish a far-wing return while the two field keepers occupy different approaches?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing one bay does not remove the keeper from the other.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: A starting return lane can separate two independently retained regions.
design.mastery: Earn territory on both sides without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same central lane supports two different enclosure rhythms.
design.routeDecision: Work one bay to completion or alternate sides to follow the safer keeper positions?

design.captureConsequence: A pad connection creates a return beyond a frame arm; retaining enemies still determine which side fills.
design.counterplay: Use an adjacent pad for a short closure, observe the keepers across all three aisles, and depart behind the outer patrol.
design.lesson: The four reclaimed pads are real return surfaces; the central component is an impassable wall.
design.mastery: Connect all four pads without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The open frame arms turn four pads into a choice of changing approach directions.
design.routeDecision: Connect an offset motor pad through the inner aisle, or circle a frame arm for a wider enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: Filling beside one arm removes old edges and changes the patrol route around the other.
design.counterplay: Watch the marked patrol, return to the broad elbow, and keep the outside approach available.
design.lesson: A frontier patrol follows the changed field edge; its speed does not increase when the route gets shorter.
design.mastery: Connect both ends of the elbow to the outer perimeter without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same L-shaped return becomes a different departure after its inside corner is captured.
design.routeDecision: Close a short cut at the elbow, or use the long arm to redirect the frontier before the next departure?

design.captureConsequence: The captured part loses its arrows and becomes ordinary reclaimed movement, so the return trip uses a different route budget.
design.counterplay: Read the far landing before accelerating. The wide marked approach has no required turn at its end; the next direction stays your choice.
design.lesson: Arrows change craft speed only while moving on unclaimed cells: faster with, slower against, unchanged across. They never push a stopped craft.
design.mastery: Reclaim both marked fields completely and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The marked center route disappears behind a stopped craft while neighboring arrows remain.
design.routeDecision: Take the marked run to the central landing, or a shorter unmarked slice near the western platform?

design.captureConsequence: The upper-petal closure leaves the western field broad; the dot-first closure shifts the surviving keeper regions toward the outer petal chain.
design.counterplay: Stage on the central landing for the upper petal, or watch the west keeper before committing to the dot. Each route preserves another safe return if the next read changes.
design.lesson: Five familiar landings form an open spiral, petal and dot rhythm; the finale adds no mandatory mechanic.
design.mastery: Complete both the central-petal and dot-first approaches without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A Lemko-pysanka-informed floral rhythm opens into a central spiral shoulder and four deliberately uneven outer landings.
design.routeDecision: Secure the upper petal from the central spiral shoulder, or connect the western dot first and build an outside return before separating the three keepers?

design.captureConsequence: One keeper retains only the region it occupies at closure.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: Reaching reclaimed ground secures a live line; empty regions fill.
design.mastery: Close a cut without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The first enclosure reveals a broad part of the horizon.
design.routeDecision: Cross to the far rail or turn back to the near rail?

design.captureConsequence: A reclaimed neck removes its speed penalty and changes the value of the next central crossing.
design.counterplay: Compare the keeper positions with both nearby landings. Cross an arrow band at right angles when its direction is unhelpful.
design.lesson: Shortest distance and shortest exposure need not be the same. Across an arrow is ordinary speed, not a sideways push.
design.mastery: Reclaim both central necks and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: An initially awkward against-arrow route becomes the best ordinary-speed connection after capture.
design.routeDecision: Use the short central neck against the lower arrows or take the longer lateral approach with them?

design.captureConsequence: The shield stays disabled after a life loss. The Sentinel remains a field anchor until its explicit release, which secures the remaining unclaimed picture.
design.counterplay: The chamber walls block movement and never close a cut. Plan the complete return through the opening. Watch both perimeter and frontier patrols when repositioning between attempts.
design.lesson: A shield capture opens a deliberate transition, not an immediate victory. After the vertical attack, close eight fresh trail cells during CORE OPEN or isolate the core.
design.mastery: Release the core in its first exposed opening and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The horizontal shield attack gives way to a vertical core attack after the first relay.
design.routeDecision: Secure an approach to the upper side of the chamber opening, or the lower side, before turning a cut around the enclosed shield?

design.captureConsequence: One pilot’s enclosure removes a material penalty and opens a full-speed route that the partner can use for the next cut.
design.counterplay: Enclose the lethal crossing before either pilot enters it. Use the west spine for shorter banks, then protect the partner’s longer approach through the newly reclaimed corridor.
design.lesson: The Disruptor creates the keeper window for a material enclosure while the Interceptor protects the exposed partner. Neutralized terrain becomes ordinary shared ground.
design.mastery: Neutralize both material beds with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: One partner opens the marked crossing while the other turns a slow approach into ordinary shared ground.
design.routeDecision: Split the outer bypasses to enclose both material beds, or first link a shared return through the slow approach?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing either anchor both protects its cell and opens a non-scoring connector. Earned side shortcuts remain vulnerable to warned erosion.
design.counterplay: Do not treat every field contact as a travelling impact. Only the marked carrier sends sparks; the eroder still breaks a live trail immediately. Use the broad center corridor to change your approach.
design.lesson: A territory repair and a carrier closure race are familiar but different decisions. Permanent foundations, opened connectors and captured objective anchors protect the planned return.
design.mastery: Traverse both opened connectors before clearing without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: An opened T-shaped return stays intact while a nearby earned edge is reopened.
design.routeDecision: Open the upper protected link first, or invest in the lower anchor while the carrier and eroder occupy different corridors?

design.captureConsequence: Relay corners stay permanent while erosion can restore a marked inner spoke. Trail impacts still disappear when a valid closure secures the trail.
design.counterplay: Enclose the lethal patches and complete the permanent corner circuit first. Repair an inner spoke only when it shortens the next closure; the durable outer route prevents reopened cells from becoming compulsory cleanup.
design.lesson: This optional combination uses only known roles. The protected circuit and earned spokes have different erosion consequences; neither changes the capture contract.
design.mastery: Traverse both opened corners and neutralize both lethal patches before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: Two missing corners become a complete durable circuit around a changing interior.
design.routeDecision: Complete the protected outer circuit through relay corners, or use the shorter marked center while field threats remain on opposite sides?

design.captureConsequence: The route both neutralizes material and changes the frontier leading to the far landing.
design.counterplay: The first island is outside the slow bed; wait there and choose the next approach deliberately.
design.lesson: A slow crossing extends trail exposure while the familiar frontier patrol keeps moving.
design.mastery: Link both landings without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A wide enclosure can remove a slow approach and redirect patrol pressure at once.
design.routeDecision: Bridge the slow center for a large enclosure, or link the landings by a longer clear route?

design.captureConsequence: The landing becomes a repeatable shortcut without changing which field enemies retain their regions.
design.counterplay: First connect the nearby landing. When an impact appears, close on reclaimed ground before it reaches the craft; a hit at the live endpoint gives no grace.
design.lesson: Only the bolt-shaped carrier sends moving impacts. Ordinary keepers still damage the trail immediately.
design.mastery: Close a cut with an active travelling impact without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A travelling impact disappears when a short return closes in time.
design.routeDecision: Use the landing as a short return, or pass it for a larger enclosure with more exposed trail?

design.captureConsequence: A line-only link can still shorten both routes while occupied regions remain unclaimed.
design.counterplay: The upper and lower keepers leave different departure windows. Use the intermediate islands to shorten exposure; a wall is never a return.
design.lesson: The return one partner builds is also a launch point for the other.
design.mastery: Connect both intermediate islands to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: An offset chain of four islands becomes one shared route network.
design.routeDecision: Take separate stepping stones, or connect across the centre before spreading out?

design.captureConsequence: An outer enclosure can remove a garden and an approach together, giving the other craft a full-speed return.
design.counterplay: Keep the lethal gardens outside your route until they are reclaimed. Time the central keeper before attempting a shared bridge.
design.lesson: A short route through slow field can keep a trail exposed longer than an outer bypass.
design.mastery: Neutralize every slow and lethal patch with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Two dangerous gardens become ordinary shared ground around a contested middle island.
design.routeDecision: Link through a slow approach to reach the middle island, or split the outer routes and clear the gardens first?

design.captureConsequence: One closure can clear a travelling impact and open a permanent connection, but the emitter still retains its field.
design.counterplay: Close before the marked lane fires, then use the new connection while preserving space from an activated roamer.
design.lesson: Combine established relay, lane and impact rules. Opening a link changes return choices, not enemy attack periods.
design.mastery: Open a connector on a cut carrying an active impact and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: An opened link provides a fresh launch point after a narrow closure escapes a known lane attack.
design.routeDecision: Spend the next attack window opening a new escape connection or enclose a smaller region while keeping the roamer dormant?

design.captureConsequence: The courtyard and outside field retain their own keeper; neither fills for free.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: A ring foundation offers inward and outward departures with different return distances.
design.mastery: Complete an inward cut and an outward cut.
design.memorableMoment: The same return ring changes meaning when approached from the other side.
design.routeDecision: Clear the enclosed courtyard first or build outward from its outer edge?

design.captureConsequence: A completed chamber contributes earned territory without automatically clearing the other occupied chambers.
design.counterplay: Reposition along the broad cross; the four field keepers cannot leave their starting chambers without a field connection.
design.lesson: Each occupied chamber retains its own field. Permanent cross lanes provide returns but do not earn coverage.
design.mastery: Make captures in three different starting chambers without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same central crossing lets the player choose the order of unequal spatial problems.
design.routeDecision: Start with a small near quadrant, or use the spacious cross to tackle the larger region while its keeper is distant?

design.captureConsequence: A short passage connection can make the far band easier to approach without changing patrol domain.
design.counterplay: Use the internal return strips while the outside patrol passes; keep one passage available for the next cut.
design.lesson: Repeated bands do not repeat the same route: their openings alternate sides.
design.mastery: Close a cut through each of the two inner passages.
design.memorableMoment: A left-to-right crossing becomes a right-to-left problem at the next band.
design.routeDecision: Cross at the staggered inner passage, or circle the end of the textile-like band for a larger enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: A side connection changes the nearby patrol frontier, while a shoulder enclosure establishes an exterior return. Open wall sections remain walls and do not create a separate capture rule.
design.counterplay: Leave from the side away from the frontier patrol. Read the inside keeper before the right-side cut, or use the visible shoulder gap to reach the longer outside approach.
design.lesson: Inspect the wall above the starting reclaimed pad. The open stepped shell blocks movement but is not a return surface; only keeper positions decide retained field, and the frontier patrol follows reclaimed edges.
design.mastery: Use both the side opening and northern shoulder approach before clearing without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The short side opening and longer stepped shoulder lead to different useful return surfaces around the same open egg silhouette.
design.routeDecision: Connect through the broad right-side opening and reshape the nearby frontier, or pass around the northern shoulder to establish the exterior left return first?

design.captureConsequence: Capture order determines which branch remains a convenient return under pressure.
design.counterplay: Use the broad central branch to switch sides; leave another return available before enlarging the roamer’s domain.
design.lesson: An escape corridor needs a usable departure, not merely a connection to reclaimed cells occupied by a roamer.
design.mastery: Connect both outer platforms and neutralize the marked pocket without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The best next capture opens a way out rather than maximizing immediate area.
design.routeDecision: Build an outside escape to the near platform, or neutralize the marked pocket before joining the far platform?

design.captureConsequence: The first captured area becomes the return surface for a shorter second cut.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: Longer exposed routes can earn more ground, but the keeper chooses which region remains.
design.mastery: Complete the mission in three cuts or fewer.
design.memorableMoment: A cautious first cut changes the best route for the next one.
design.routeDecision: Take the nearby narrow slice now, or travel along the rail for a larger enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: The relay adds a non-scoring permanent return; erosion may restore arrows only on the earned side routes.
design.counterplay: Use the protected connector as a fallback and follow erosion and lane warnings. Neither forces a repair before another route is available.
design.lesson: Combine known arrow, erosion and relay rules: foundations and opened connectors are permanent; earned marked territory can reactivate.
design.mastery: Use the protected connector and reclaim both side currents before clearing without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: The center connector stays dependable while a reopened current visibly changes a side route.
design.routeDecision: Secure the permanent return first or invest in an earned sideways shortcut that erosion may reopen into an arrow field?

design.captureConsequence: Neutralizing either outer thread changes the best route to the middle platform; the remaining occupied field still requires a deliberate closure.
design.counterplay: The long side spines offer many departures. Go above or below the walls, never into the lethal notches; the central keeper preserves the middle until isolated.
design.lesson: A partner can turn a slow approach into a fast shared return before the second cut begins.
design.mastery: Neutralize every material patch and connect the middle platform to the perimeter, with closures from both craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Two winding approaches become one short route through the reclaimed middle.
design.routeDecision: Weave around opposite wall tips to bank the middle, or clear one material lane and share that approach?

design.captureConsequence: The first bridge changes return distance while the outer route remains fixed.
design.counterplay: Both landings offer return choices without needing the pickup.
design.lesson: Touch the optional life pickup on reclaimed ground; enclosing it is not collection.
design.mastery: Use both landings before clearing.
design.memorableMoment: A deliberate detour across the landing earns a visible recovery bonus.
design.routeDecision: Use the long landing to wait out a patrol pass, or bridge to the shorter far landing?

design.captureConsequence: A rewarding capture can create both new return ground and a new threat on that ground.
design.counterplay: The first island return wakes the sleeper behind you. Watch its one-second warning, then use either side of the broad platform for your next departure.
design.lesson: A dormant roamer does not retain field. Reclaiming its full body starts a warning, then it moves and threatens reclaimed ground.
design.mastery: Activate the roamer and complete another closure without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Your first thin connection wakes a threat on the very ground you just reclaimed; the broad landing gives room to choose a way out.
design.routeDecision: Wake the sleeper on the short island connection, or build a side return before reclaiming its corridor?

design.captureConsequence: The shield stays disabled after a life loss. The Sentinel remains a field anchor until its explicit release, which secures the remaining unclaimed picture.
design.counterplay: The chamber walls block movement and never close a cut. Plan the complete return through the opening. Watch both perimeter and frontier patrols when repositioning between attempts.
design.lesson: A shield capture opens a deliberate transition, not an immediate victory. After the vertical attack, close eight fresh trail cells during CORE OPEN or isolate the core.
design.mastery: Release the core in its first exposed opening and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The horizontal shield attack gives way to a vertical core attack after the first relay.
design.routeDecision: Secure an approach to the upper side of the chamber opening, or the lower side, before turning a cut around the enclosed shield?

design.captureConsequence: The chosen enclosure changes the contour around one arm and the next useful return.
design.counterplay: Use the broad L-shaped foundation to change approach; the optional slow pickup is not required.
design.lesson: Practice changing a frontier route before combining it with an outer patrol.
design.mastery: Close from both arms without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A new return draws the frontier patrol around a different side of the L.
design.routeDecision: Extend the short arm to redirect contour pressure, or reach around the long arm for more ground?

design.captureConsequence: A bridge between lanes creates a new return and can move the contour across the next intended approach.
design.counterplay: The upper and lower gaps stay wide; wait on a foundation and choose the side away from patrol pressure.
design.lesson: Staggered return lanes reward planning the next departure, not just reaching the nearest reclaimed cell.
design.mastery: Join all three return lanes without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: One diagonal-looking route is executed as clear orthogonal cuts between staggered platforms.
design.routeDecision: Alternate the broad top and bottom connections, or take a slow central link to reshape the frontier sooner?

design.captureConsequence: An inner landing shortens a later cut without banking against a wall. Outer returns introduce reclaimed-ground pressure, and two retainers keep each chamber contested until deliberately enclosed.
design.counterplay: The top and bottom baffle ends stay open. Watch both local keepers before crossing; after waking a roamer, turn onto a different return rather than waiting on its new rail. Either partner may travel around the divider to help.
design.lesson: Each chamber offers a short changing return and a longer inner connection; opening one chamber never clears the other occupied field.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers, with each craft closing in its starting chamber and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: A quick outside escape and a protected inner receiver become two different ways to reopen the same depot.
design.routeDecision: Wake the outer return patrols for quick perimeter access, or wrap the inner baffles to establish receiver landings first?

design.captureConsequence: Material neutralization and roamer activation can occur in the same enclosure; both partners must read the changed board.
design.counterplay: Use the side spines to change departure heights. Enclose crosses before entering them and leave space around the courtyard when a roamer wakes.
design.lesson: Removing a terrain hazard does not make every reclaimed route free of enemies.
design.mastery: Activate both roamers and connect the courtyard to the perimeter, with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: A dangerous garden becomes passable just as the tracked bodies make the surrounding ground busy.
design.routeDecision: Neutralize the upper hazard before linking the courtyard, or establish the lower slow-field approach while the partner prepares a different exit?

design.captureConsequence: A capture changes your return options but can create an eligible frontier for erosion.
design.counterplay: Watch the eroder stop and mark a cell. Keep a permanent return within reach instead of chasing every lost cell.
design.lesson: The marked cell warns before reopening. Foundations remain permanent; earned ground can need repair.
design.mastery: Repair an eroded cell with a legal closure without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A small gap reopens beside a landing that stays intact.
design.routeDecision: Use the permanent landing for repeated returns, or bank a larger exposed edge that the eroder can reopen?

design.captureConsequence: A line-only first cut establishes a permanent return lane for later enclosures.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: Two occupied regions can keep their field even though the closing line is reclaimed.
design.mastery: Create and then use a line-only return lane.
design.memorableMoment: The board explains why both occupied sides remain dark.
design.routeDecision: Separate the two keepers first or wait until they share one side?

design.captureConsequence: The two original gates become the same permanent, unscored connectors. Each earns a useful launch beside a different wall opening, so relay order changes the next approach rather than merely collecting two markers.
design.counterplay: Go around the wall above the west landing to enclose its relay. After opening that bridge, the middle platform offers a shorter approach around the eastern lower hook; the outer rail remains a longer alternative.
design.lesson: The open vytynanka-inspired vase forms are walls around capture links. Each relay still opens only its own permanent connector; the shapes do not create new triggers or return surfaces.
design.mastery: Open the eastern connector before the western connector, using its upper opening, and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A relay reached from outside the first open vase turns the middle landing into the inside approach to the second.
design.routeDecision: Enclose the near relay around its open vase shoulder and use the earned middle launch, or reach the eastern trigger around its upper negative-space opening from the boundary first?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing a new inner return does not redirect the outer patrol.
design.counterplay: The first island offers an interior return while the patrol stays on the outside rail.
design.lesson: Reclaimed ground closes a cut, but the outer patrol can still hit the craft there.
design.mastery: Complete without touching the outer patrol.
design.memorableMoment: A return inside the board avoids a dangerous stretch of the outer rail.
design.routeDecision: Leave before the outer patrol approaches, or wait for it to pass and return behind it?

design.captureConsequence: A successful enclosure turns the dangerous center into a new traversable return surface.
design.counterplay: The first return and broad outside approaches avoid the marked bed entirely.
design.lesson: Framed crosses harm the craft on unclaimed field. Capturing that field neutralizes the hazard.
design.mastery: Neutralize the whole central bed without visiting the far landing first.
design.memorableMoment: The crossed warning disappears from earned ground without changing the underlying map rule.
design.routeDecision: Enclose the marked central bed before crossing, or keep a longer clear path around it?

design.captureConsequence: Closure cancels the committed attack. Field-retaining enemies still determine which regions remain unclaimed, and the existing terrain or patrol consequences remain active.
design.counterplay: Use the dogleg to break line of sight, wait through the finite commitment, and cross each occupied chamber toward its nearest genuine return.
design.lesson: Physical walls and reclaimed ground block sensing; the dogleg closes cuts, but a wall alone never becomes a return surface.
design.mastery: Make a closure in both starting chambers and neutralize the lower lethal pocket without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: The same stepped structure first screens pursuit and then closes a cut at a different height.
design.routeDecision: Screen the upper route behind the dogleg before a larger enclosure, or clear the lower chamber first and keep the central step as an emergency return?

design.captureConsequence: Capturing a relay joins its store to the spine and gives a shorter later departure without mandatory corridor cleanup.
design.counterplay: Use the open side of each store to enclose a trigger instead of tracing every bend of the structure.
design.lesson: A shortcut changes return distance, not the meaning of the surrounding open field. Broad exits remain available before either relay.
design.mastery: Open both shortcuts within two consecutive captures and clear without a life loss.
design.memorableMoment: An apparently winding route becomes a direct permanent connection after one deliberate enclosure.
design.routeDecision: Break the western inward route at the top or the eastern route at the bottom before moving across the central spine?

design.captureConsequence: The route both neutralizes material and changes the frontier leading to the far landing.
design.counterplay: The first island is outside the slow bed; wait there and choose the next approach deliberately.
design.lesson: A slow crossing extends trail exposure while the familiar frontier patrol keeps moving.
design.mastery: Link both landings without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: A wide enclosure can remove a slow approach and redirect patrol pressure at once.
design.routeDecision: Bridge the slow center for a large enclosure, or link the landings by a longer clear route?

design.captureConsequence: One closure can remove a garden and its slow approach, opening a full-speed route that the other craft can use for the next enclosure.
design.counterplay: Assign the Interceptor to the exposed bridge and the Disruptor to the keeper nearest the chosen garden. Enclose lethal terrain instead of crossing it; the resulting reclaimed approach is useful to both craft.
design.lesson: Interceptor Support protects exposed Team lines while Disruptor Support slows the keeper guarding a material enclosure. A completed enclosure neutralizes its terrain for either partner.
design.mastery: Neutralize every slow and lethal patch with a closure from each craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Two dangerous gardens become ordinary shared ground around a contested middle island.
design.routeDecision: Link through a slow approach to reach the middle island, or split the outer routes and clear the gardens first?

design.captureConsequence: Neutralized vertical links simplify later travel, but the stationary emitter still retains field and follows the same attack schedule.
design.counterplay: Stage on a broad platform; wait out the lower lane warning without drawing, then choose a return above it or through its recovery.
design.lesson: Arrow speed changes travel time, not attack warnings or enemy speed. Read the full route and the next landing before using a window.
design.mastery: Reclaim the east and west marked links and clear without losing a life.
design.memorableMoment: Opposing long lanes stop being asymmetric after they are reclaimed.
design.routeDecision: Use the short alternating vertical links or make a wider unmarked capture during a visible lane-emitter recovery?

design.captureConsequence: New links change route length; the keepers still determine which regions fill.
design.counterplay: Watch each keeper before departing; close early when its path threatens the line.
design.lesson: Connected islands turn one long exposure into several shorter decisions.
design.mastery: Connect all three islands before the clear.
design.memorableMoment: A chain of small connections makes the broad final enclosure possible.
design.routeDecision: Join successive islands for short returns or bypass one for a larger enclosure?

design.captureConsequence: Neutralizing either outer thread changes the best route to the middle platform; the remaining occupied field still requires a deliberate closure.
design.counterplay: The long side spines offer many departures. Go above or below the walls, never into the lethal notches; the central keeper preserves the middle until isolated.
design.lesson: A partner can turn a slow approach into a fast shared return before the second cut begins.
design.mastery: Neutralize every material patch and connect the middle platform to the perimeter, with closures from both craft and no knockdowns.
design.memorableMoment: Two winding approaches become one short route through the reclaimed middle.
design.routeDecision: Weave around opposite wall tips to bank the middle, or clear one material lane and share that approach?
